newsitem.title: FRANCE: NATO's Solana reassures Moscow on enlargement.
newsitem.headline: NATO's Solana reassures Moscow on enlargement.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana sought on Thursday to reassure Russia about alliance plans for enlargement, but acknowledged time would be needed to convince Moscow they were not designed to harm it.

"A European security architecture worth its name must be one that gives the largest European state, Russia, its rightful place and enables Russia to make its full contribution," Solana told the Council of Europe's parliamentary assembly.

"The opening of NATO is therefore in no sense aimed at isolating or marginalising Russia," Solana said, adding: "Clearly, it will take time to make Russia fully understand that the opening of NATO is not aimed against her."
Solana said that at its next summit on July 8-9 in Madrid, NATO would invite one or perhaps several countries to join the alliance by 1999.
In an interview with Bonn's General-Anzeiger daily published on Thursday, Solana said he was worried Russia was misunderstanding the alliance's intentions on its future enlargement.

NATO countries plan to name new members from central and eastern Europe at the Madrid summit, arguing that -- despite Moscow's virulent opposition -- the alliance's enlargement will help defuse potential regional flashpoints.
Critics of enlargement say it could end up having a destabilising effect, creating a new division in Europe.

NATO diplomats hailed Primakov's confirmation of a new meeting as further evidence Solana had been accepted by Moscow as the West's main negotiator on a new pact or charter covering all relations between the old Cold War enemies.
"It is good news for Solana, he seems to have succeeded in convincing the Russians he is the man to deal with," said one alliance diplomat.

The first round of talks, held in Moscow on January 20, made no progress in narrowing the gap between the two over the alliance's to grant membership to countries such as Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.

Since then, however, the allies have stepped up diplomatic efforts to entice the Russians into a deal by hinting at concessions on outstanding arms control issues and dangling carrots of more financial aid.
